passages.happening:
“Now Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu took their censers, put fire in them and added incense, and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, contrary to His command” (verse 1).

“So fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed them, and they died in the presence of the LORD” (verse 2).

Moses says to Aaron, “This is what the LORD meant when He said: ‘To those who come near Me I will show My holiness, and in the sight of all the people I will reveal My glory.’” Then the text adds, “But Aaron remained silent” (verse 3).

Moses calls two cousins of the dead men to carry the bodies out of the camp, still in their tunics (verses 4-5). He tells Aaron and his two remaining sons not to show the signs of mourning and not to leave the tent, “for the LORD’s anointing oil is on you” (verse 7). “But your brothers, the whole house of Israel, may mourn on account of the fire that the LORD has ignited” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The chapter before ended in joy. Fire came from the LORD and took the offering, and the people shouted and fell on their faces. This chapter happens on the same day. The same words come back, with a terrible change: ‘fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed’ (9:24; 10:2). The first time it took the offering. This time it takes two priests.

Nadab and Abihu were not minor figures. They were Aaron's two eldest sons. They had gone up Mount Sinai with Moses and the elders, and there ‘they saw the God of Israel’ (Exodus 24:10).

A censer was a pan for carrying live coals. Incense was sprinkled on the coals to make a fragrant smoke. The Hebrew word for their fire is zarah: strange, foreign, outside what was laid down. The whole of chapters 8 and 9 kept saying that everything was done ‘as the LORD had commanded’. Verse 1 says this was done ‘contrary to His command’. Word for word the Hebrew says: which he had not commanded them.

The saying Moses quotes gives the event its meaning. God shows his holiness in those who come near him. The priests stood closest to him, and on the first day of Israel's worship the line between God's holiness and human presumption was drawn where everyone could see it.

The Bible often sets a sudden failure straight after a new beginning: the garden, the golden calf at the foot of Sinai, and in the church's first days Ananias and Sapphira.

Then the grief. Loose hair and torn clothes were the ordinary signs of mourning. Aaron and his remaining sons are told not to make them, because they are still in the middle of their service, with the anointing oil on them. But the grief is not forbidden. It is handed to the people. All Israel is to mourn for these two men, in the priests' place.

And Aaron is silent. The Hebrew verb can mean to be still. Readers have heard in his silence a father stunned by grief, a man bowing to God's judgment, or a man with nothing he can say. The text reports it and adds no comment.
passages.later:
The book of Numbers records the deaths in a list of Aaron's family, and adds that the two had no sons (Numbers 3:4).

When the Day of Atonement is given, the text looks back to this day: “Now the LORD spoke to Moses after the death of two of Aaron’s sons when they approached the presence of the LORD” (Leviticus 16:1). What follows there explains how the high priest may come near and live.

The letter to the Hebrews keeps both sides of this chapter. It tells Christians to ‘worship God acceptably with reverence and awe’, and gives the reason: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:28-29). And it invites them to come close: “Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence” (Hebrews 4:16).
passages.hard:
Why were Nadab and Abihu killed for what looks like a mistake in a ritual?

The text gives only one explanation. They offered fire ‘contrary to His command’. Readers since ancient times have tried to say more exactly what the fault was. Some think the fire was not taken from the altar, where the coals were supposed to come from. Some think the two went further into the tent than they were allowed, since chapter 16 recalls their deaths when it limits entry to the innermost room. Some link the story with the rule about wine that follows in verse 9, and suggest they had been drinking. Others see pride: acting on their own, on the very day the priesthood began. The text leaves the details open. In every one of these readings the heart of it is the same. They treated the presence of God as something they could come to in whatever way they chose.

The severity also belongs to the moment. This was the founding day of Israel's worship, and the priests, who stood closest to God, were held to the highest standard. The Bible shows judgments like this at other beginnings: Uzzah and the ark (2 Samuel 6:6-7), Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5). They are rare. They are never presented as God's usual way with his people. The offerings of chapters 4 and 5 were given to cover his people's ordinary failures.

None of this makes the passage easy, and it should not be made easy. Leviticus itself does not make the grief small. A father stands silent, and a whole nation is told to mourn. Readers who find the chapter hard are in the company of the text.

So this story must not be turned into a threat held over ordinary worshipers, as though God were waiting to strike anyone who makes a mistake in church. It is about two priests on one day, and the book around it is full of God's provision for people who get things wrong.

Nadab and Abihu had a mother too. Her name was Elisheba (Exodus 6:23), and the chapter does not tell us what she felt. If you have lost a child, or carry a grief like hers, please do not carry it alone. Speak to someone you trust, a pastor or a grief counsellor, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Two men who had seen God came to him in a way of their own choosing. Ask where you have grown so used to holy things that you handle them carelessly. And notice Aaron's silence, and the nation told to grieve for him. Ask who near you is carrying a grief they cannot show, and how you could carry some of it for them.

passages.happening:
“Then the LORD said to Aaron” (verse 8). The priests are not to drink wine or strong drink when they go into the Tent of Meeting, “or else you will die; this is a permanent statute for the generations to come” (verse 9).

“You must distinguish between the holy and the common, between the clean and the unclean, so that you may teach the Israelites all the statutes that the LORD has given them through Moses” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
Almost everywhere in this book God speaks to Moses. Here he speaks to Aaron alone. It is one of the few such speeches in the Torah, and it comes on the day Aaron has lost two sons. God does not leave the grieving father out. He speaks to him directly and gives him his work.

The rule about drink is about a clear head. It is tied to two tasks.

The first is to tell things apart: holy from common, clean from unclean. The Hebrew verb is the one used in Genesis 1, where God separates light from darkness and waters from waters. The priests are to carry on that work of making order. The next five chapters, on food, childbirth, skin disease and bodily discharges, are the content of it.

The second task is to teach. Priests in Israel were not only men who offered sacrifices. They were teachers, and a people's grasp of God's ways depended on them. Verse 11 is among the clearest statements of that in the Bible.

This rule is not a ban on wine for everyone. Wine was part of Israel's meals and offerings. It applies to the priests ‘when you enter the Tent of Meeting’.
passages.later:
Ezekiel repeats both parts for the priests of a restored temple: “No priest may drink wine before he enters the inner court” (Ezekiel 44:21), and “They are to teach My people the difference between the holy and the common” (Ezekiel 44:23).

Malachi held the priests of his day to verse 11: “For the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth” (Malachi 2:7).

Paul asks something similar of a leader in the church: he is to be ‘temperate, self-controlled’ and ‘not dependent on wine’ (1 Timothy 3:2-3).
passages.asks: On the worst day of Aaron's life, God spoke to him by name and trusted him with work. Ask whether you believe God still has something for you to do after a great loss or a great failure. And if you teach others about God, in a home or a church, ask what clouds your judgment, and what would keep it clear.

passages.t: The priests' food, and a goat not eaten
passages.happening:
Moses tells Aaron and his remaining sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, to eat what is left of the grain offering beside the altar, “because it is most holy” (verse 12). They and their sons and daughters may eat the breast and the thigh of the peace offerings in any clean place (verse 14).

Then Moses looks for the goat of the people's sin offering and finds that it has been burned. He is angry. “Why didn’t you eat the sin offering in the holy place?” (verse 17).

Aaron answers. “Since these things have happened to me, if I had eaten the sin offering today, would it have been acceptable in the sight of the LORD?” (verse 19).

“And when Moses heard this explanation, he was satisfied” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The day is not over, and the service has to go on. Moses makes sure the priests still receive their food. The deaths have not undone their place.

Then comes a dispute. Chapter 6 laid down that a sin offering whose blood was not carried into the tent must be eaten by the priests. This goat's blood was not carried in. So the priests should have eaten it. They burned it.

After what has just happened, Moses is alarmed at any departure from what was commanded. He is angry, and it is easy to see why.

Aaron's answer is quiet. His sons died that day. How could he sit down and eat the holy meal as if nothing had happened? Would God have been pleased with that? He is not being careless about the rule. He is asking what fits a day like this.

And Moses accepts it. That is unusual. In the same chapter where two priests die for doing what was not commanded, a grieving father departs from the letter of a command, gives his reason, and is not condemned. The chapter does not explain how the two fit together. It sets them side by side. The first was men coming to God on their own terms. The second is a man who cannot eat for grief, and who fears to treat a holy thing lightly.
passages.later:
The prophets drew a line that this scene already suggests, between worship done from the heart and worship that is only outward. Through Hosea God says, “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings” (Hosea 6:6).

The letter to the Hebrews says of Israel's high priest that he “is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided, since he himself is beset by weakness” (Hebrews 5:2). Aaron ends this day as that kind of priest.
passages.asks: Moses was angry, listened to the answer, and let it stand. Ask whether you can be corrected by someone you have just rebuked. And ask whether you make room, in your home or your church, for people who cannot do today what they would do on an ordinary day.
